hints: Look closely at Fig. 3.1 - find what joins one circle to the next in the long chain, and then find the different S-S links that staple distant parts together.
walkthrough:
Spot the Two Different Covalent Links**
Lysozyme is a polypeptide, so neighbouring amino acids in the chain are joined by peptide bonds formed by condensation. In Fig. 3.1 you can also see four S-S bridges labelled between cysteine residues - these are disulfide bonds that hold folds together.
Final answer: Peptide bonds and disulfide bonds.

hints: Think about what is simplest about Fig. 3.1 - it just shows beads in a line in a particular running order, before any folding is considered.
walkthrough:
What Primary Means**
Primary structure is the most basic level of protein structure. It is simply which amino acids are present and in what order they are linked by peptide bonds to make the polypeptide, for example Lys-Val-Phe-Gly and so on as shown around the chain in Fig. 3.1.
Final answer: The sequence / order of amino acids in the polypeptide chain.

hints: Break the word apart - hydro means water and lysis means splitting - so think about what water does to a chemical bond.
walkthrough:
Water Splits the Bond**
In hydrolysis, a water molecule is used to break a covalent bond such as a glycosidic bond. One part of the substrate gains -H and the other gains -OH from the water, so the large molecule is split into smaller units.
Final answer: Breaking of a (covalent) bond by the addition of water.

hints: Recall what unique polymer gives bacterial walls their strength and contains sugars linked by glycosidic bonds plus short amino acid chains.
walkthrough:
Link Wall Chemistry to the Enzyme**
Bacterial cell walls are strengthened by peptidoglycan, also called murein. It is made of polysaccharide chains with amino sugars joined by beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds cross-linked by short peptides, so this is the natural substrate that lysozyme hydrolyses.
Final answer: Peptidoglycan (murein).

hints: Start by picturing how induced fit differs from a rigid lock and key - is the active site a perfect match before the substrate arrives?
Think about what the active site itself does when the substrate touches it - which part moves?
Consider what the result of that movement is for the fit and for bringing R-groups into position.
Finish by linking that close interaction to formation of the complex and to making the reaction go faster.
walkthrough:
Not a Perfect Fit at First**
In induced fit the substrate shape is not exactly complementary to the active site shape before binding. This is different from the older lock and key idea of a rigid perfect match.

Active Site Moulds Around Substrate**
The active site is partially flexible. When the substrate enters, the active site changes shape slightly to mould around it.

Complementary Complex Forms**
That movement makes the active site and substrate now complementary, giving a better fit. This allows an enzyme-substrate complex (ESC) to form with many points of contact.

Catalysis Through Close Contact**
R-groups in the active site are now correctly positioned to interact with the substrate, stressing bonds and lowering the activation energy ($E_A$). The substrate reacts to form products which then leave.

Final answer: Substrate shape is not exactly complementary to active site; active site is flexible and changes shape slightly on substrate binding; active site and substrate become complementary / better fit; enzyme-substrate complex forms; interaction with R-groups lowers activation energy so products form.

hints: Break extra- and cellular apart - where are tears and saliva in relation to the cells that made the enzyme?
walkthrough:
Outside the Cell**
Extracellular means outside the cell. Lysozyme is made inside cells lining glands but is secreted into tears and saliva where it acts on bacteria, so its site of action is external to the cells that produce it.
Final answer: Outside cells / secreted out of cells to act externally.

hints: On Fig. 3.2 find the flat plateau where rate stops rising, then trace straight down to read the first concentration where that plateau is reached.
walkthrough:
Read Vmax Then Read Across**
The maximum rate $V_{max}$ is the plateau at about $3.2 \text{ } \mu \text{mol min}^{-1}$. Move along the curve until it first becomes flat - this occurs at about $3.0 \text{ mmol}$ on the x-axis. The lowest concentration to give $V_{max}$ is therefore about $2.9 \text{ mmol}$.
Final answer: Approx $2.9 \text{ mmol}$ (accept $2.75-3.0 \text{ mmol}$) substrate concentration.

hints: Remember $K_m$ is the substrate concentration that gives half of $V_{max}$ - so first halve the plateau rate you found, then read the matching x-value.
walkthrough:
Halve Vmax and Read Off**
$V_{max}$ is about $3.2 \text{ } \mu \text{mol min}^{-1}$, so half $V_{max}$ is about $1.6 \text{ } \mu \text{mol min}^{-1}$. Find $1.6$ on the y-axis of Fig. 3.2, read across to the curve and down to the x-axis. This gives a substrate concentration of $1 \text{ mmol}$, which is $K_m$.
Final answer: $K_m = 1 \text{ mmol}$.

hints: Think about what a competitive inhibitor does at low substrate - it occupies active sites, so for any given substrate concentration will the rate be higher or lower?
Think about what happens at very high substrate concentration when huge numbers of substrate molecules outcompete the inhibitor - can the original maximum still be reached?
walkthrough:
Lower Rate at First**
A competitive inhibitor binds reversibly to the active site, so fewer enzyme molecules are available to substrate. Draw a single smooth curve starting at the origin but always below the original curve, showing a lower gradient and lower rate for the same substrate concentration.

Same Vmax at High Substrate**
At very high substrate concentration the substrate outcompetes the inhibitor, so all active sites can still be filled. The curve must therefore rise to meet the same plateau, $V_{max}$ of about $3.2 \text{ } \mu \text{mol min}^{-1}$, just reaching it at a higher substrate concentration.
Final answer: Curve with lower gradient than original at all lower substrate concentrations but reaching the same $V_{max}$ plateau (approx $3.2 \text{ } \mu \text{mol min}^{-1}$).
